---
title: "Learning Moment: `.nojekyll` and `make publish`"
date: 2026-10-30
categories: [claude, learning, ai-collaboration, github, quarto, over-engineering, documentation]
---

## Context

The project was a course's online book, written with Quarto
and published to GitHub Pages from the `gh-pages` branch.
Two GitHub Actions workflows did the work:

- `publish.yml` rendered the book into `docs/` on every push to `main`
  and published it with `quarto publish gh-pages`.
- `pr.yml` rendered the book on every pull request,
  so that changes could be checked before they were merged.

The task was to give every pull request a live preview of the rendered book,
using [pr-preview-action](https://github.com/rossjrw/pr-preview-action).
It pushes each pull request's build to the `gh-pages` branch under `pr-preview/pr-<N>/`
and comments the link on the pull request.

Claude had already written a first version.
It used two jobs: one built the book on the macOS runner the book always used,
and a second, on Ubuntu, deployed the preview.
The split rested on an assumption Claude had not checked:
that pr-preview-action, a set of bash scripts, would not run on macOS.

## The Initial Ask

Quoted as typed:

> "let's make sure the GHA workflows are pretty simple and we're using this
> https://github.com/rossjrw/pr-preview-action for quarto"

## Claude's Initial Response

Claude read the action's README and its scripts.
The scripts used nothing that macOS lacks,
so the two jobs collapsed into the single job the README shows.
That was the first assumption gone.

The README also warned that the main deployment must not delete the previews:
"If you don't do this, your main deployment may delete all of your currently-existing PR previews."
`quarto publish gh-pages` does exactly that.
It runs `git rm -r .` on the `gh-pages` branch before every publish.
So, following the README, Claude switched `publish.yml` to render the book
and deploy `docs/` with [github-pages-deploy-action](https://github.com/JamesIves/github-pages-deploy-action),
using `clean-exclude: pr-preview` (keep the previews) and `force: false` (don't force-push).

Then Claude noticed two more things, and acted on both.

**A `.nojekyll` file.**
The `gh-pages` branch had a `.nojekyll` file, which `quarto publish` had added.
It tells GitHub Pages not to run Jekyll over the site.
A local `docs/` folder had no `.nojekyll`,
and the new deploy action "cleans" files that aren't in the folder it deploys.
Claude concluded the deploy would delete the file, and added a step to recreate it:

```yaml
# tell GitHub Pages not to run Jekyll on the site (`quarto publish` used to add this)
- name: Add .nojekyll
  run: touch docs/.nojekyll
```

**The `make publish` target.**
The project's Makefile still had a `publish` target that ran `quarto publish gh-pages` locally.
That would now wipe every preview and force-push over the deploys from GitHub Actions,
so Claude removed it:

> One leftover footgun: `make publish` still runs `quarto publish gh-pages` locally.
> That would wipe every PR preview and force-push over CI's deploys.
> Since publishing now happens in CI on every push to `main`, I'll remove the target.

## The Exchange

**Turn 1 — User** (quoted as typed):

> "i think we dont' need to touch the nojekull file if there is already a nojekyll file
> in the root or in quarto project root? we aren't doing anythign to the docs directory
> for deployment all deployments are under gh-pages"

**Turn 1 — Claude:**

Claude checked before answering, this time in the deploy action's own source and README.
Its clean-up step excludes `.nojekyll` whenever the deployed folder doesn't have one:

```typescript
!fs.existsSync(`${action.folderPath}/${DefaultExcludedFiles.NOJEKYLL}`)
  ? `--exclude ${DefaultExcludedFiles.NOJEKYLL}`
  : ''
```

The README says the same thing in plain words:

> If you're using a custom domain and require a `CNAME` file,
> or if you require the use of a `.nojekyll` file,
> you can safely commit these files directly into the deployment branch
> without them being overridden after each deployment.

So the step was unnecessary, and Claude removed it.
The check also sharpened the user's reasoning.
Neither the repository root nor the Quarto project root had a `.nojekyll`.
The file that mattered was the one already on `gh-pages`,
and the deploy action leaves it alone.
The user's conclusion was right; the check showed exactly why.

**Turn 2 — User** (quoted as typed):

> "we should keep the make target for publish. but it should echo
> "no need to manually pubblish, github actions will do this for you, including branch PRs"
> or somethign liek that"

**Turn 2 — Claude:**

Claude put the target back.
Instead of publishing, it now explains where publishing happens:

```make
publish: ## No need: GitHub Actions publishes the book and PR previews
	@echo "No need to publish manually: GitHub Actions does this for you."
	@echo "  - every push to main deploys the book to GitHub Pages (.github/workflows/publish.yml)"
	@echo "  - every pull request from a branch gets a preview at pr-preview/pr-<N>/ (.github/workflows/pr.yml)"
```

`make help` lists it as
"publish  No need: GitHub Actions publishes the book and PR previews".

## The Final Solution

The publish workflow renders the book and deploys it, with no `.nojekyll` step:

```yaml
- name: Render Quarto
  uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/render@v2
  with:
    path: book

# Unlike `quarto publish`, this keeps the PR previews in pr-preview/
# and does not force-push, as the pr-preview-action README recommends.
- name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
  uses: JamesIves/github-pages-deploy-action@<pinned-sha> # v4.9.0
  with:
    folder: docs
    branch: gh-pages
    clean-exclude: pr-preview
    force: false
```

The preview workflow is one job: check out, build (skipped when the pull request closes),
then pr-preview-action, which deploys the preview or removes it.
`make publish` stays as a signpost to the two workflows.

## The Lesson

**What Claude got right:**
Claude found the real problem from the README:
`quarto publish gh-pages` wipes the `gh-pages` branch, so it would delete every preview.
It confirmed that in Quarto's own source before changing the publish workflow.
It was right that `.nojekyll` matters to GitHub Pages,
and right that a local `quarto publish` would undo what the workflows set up.

**What required human expertise:**
Two kinds of knowledge Claude didn't have.
First, how this site is actually rendered and deployed:
the render happens on the runner, and only the deploy touches `gh-pages`,
so files already on `gh-pages` stay unless something removes them.
Second, how people use the project:
collaborators, old notes and muscle memory still reach for `make publish`.
Deleting the target turns that into a bare
"No rule to make target 'publish'" with no hint of what changed.
Keeping the target and having it explain where publishing went
documents the new workflow at the moment someone needs it.

**Why Claude missed it:**
Claude made the same kind of mistake three times in one task:
it predicted a problem and patched it, instead of checking the tool that would cause it.
It read pr-preview-action's README closely,
but inferred the deploy action's behaviour from the everyday meaning of "clean"
and from a local `docs/` folder, which shows what a render produces, not what a deploy keeps.
Behind that was a migration reflex:
"`quarto publish` used to add `.nojekyll`, so the replacement must add it too."
The macOS assumption followed the same pattern.
It only surfaced because the user asked for the workflows to be simple.
For `make publish`, Claude optimized for the system (remove the footgun)
rather than for the people who use it.

**Key takeaway:**
Before adding a step to replace what a migration might break, check what the new tool already preserves,
and when you retire a command people know, make it say where the work went instead of deleting it.
